hero.kicker: Capability 04 · CMMS · Computerized Maintenance Management System
hero.h1: A maintenance system that needs no data entry.
hero.dek: The plant already knows when each machine ran, when it stopped and what the operator said about it. Maintenance should be arithmetic over that record — not a second one somebody has to keep.

sections.title: Everything the maintenance system does, in one glance.
rows: To know what maintenance owes you right now
The board opens on the debt: overdue, due today, this week, later, and what the line has asked for.
`the board`
To see the week the crew is walking into
Seven days from today, protected windows drawn as rooms, anything late pinned to today.
`the week`
To ask which machine is hurting you
One card per machine: its open jobs, its meters, mean time between failures, mean time to repair, and the downtime behind it.
`the machines wall`
To know whether the shelf will stop a job
Shortages pinned on top, each naming the jobs it is holding.
`parts`
To tell maintenance something is wrong
Raise it: the machine, what is wrong, how bad, and whether the line is down because of it.
`the board, top`
To turn a stop or an alarm into tracked work
Call maintenance on the restart receipt, or in the alarm acknowledgement: the machine, the moment and the reason ride along.
`the performance page, the alarm`
To put the work in the crew's hands
Release it: the checklist freezes on the spot and a protected window is booked.
`the job's dossier`
To do the work
Take it, start it, work the steps, finish it — on a phone, with nothing installed.
`the job screen`
To close it properly
Minutes, stopped time, what you found, why it happened, then sign.
`the close pane`
To set a machine up in one press
Choose the machine's type and dress it: its parts, its plans, their checklists, the spares each job needs and the failure words all arrive.
`the editor's maintenance room`
To say when a machine gets serviced
On a date, so many days since the last one, every so many running hours or starts, when a tag says so, after too many breakdowns — and one that follows a signed repair by itself.
`the plan pane`
To catalogue a spare or move stock
Received, taken, put back, corrected: the shelf is the sum of its movements, and the whole site's ledger is one door away.
`the store`
To prove the work was done
On time against due, the money argument, what broke and why, and every closed job as its own sheet.
`the record, then Reports`
sections.note: Every job is born a draft. The machine and the operator propose; a supervisor releases.

sections.title: The plant under it
sections.promise: It opens on a plant that is already there.

cols: Maintenance here is not a system you feed.
It is arithmetic over the plant the SCADA is already writing: the same machines, the same signals, the same alarm journal, and the same history the trends read.
Maintenance is not a product beside the SCADA here; it is a fold over the same rows.

sections.title: It opens on a plant that is already there:

screen.caption: The live line the maintenance sits on — drawn once, served on every screen.

items.lead: The same pages everywhere
items.text: The same pages follow a user from the wall panel to a phone, with nothing installed and nothing licensed per screen; three languages from one design.

items.lead: Every machine carries its own door
items.text: Tap a pump for its faceplate, its journal and its documents, from the page it stands on.

items.lead: The journal a fault is called from
items.text: Alarms prioritised, acknowledged, shelved with a reason, kept in a journal a tag delete cannot rewrite.

items.lead: The job and the alarm point at the same event
items.text: It is the journal a fault is called into maintenance from.

items.lead: TimeLens replay
items.text: Replays any screen from the history the plant already keeps: the alarms at that moment, commands off, the day's timeline, back to live.

items.lead: The Tag Lens
items.text: Shows where one signal is used — pages, trends, alarms, report blocks, conditions — before anybody renames it.

screens.caption: The Tag Lens — one signal, with every page, trend, alarm, report block and condition that uses it.
TimeLens under any replayed screen — the alarms at that moment, commands off, the day's timeline, back to live.

sections.title: The machine's type
sections.promise: One word plants the whole maintenance package.

cols: A machine arrives with a code, a name and one word: its kind.
That word carries its parts, its service plans, the steps a fitter will work through, the spares each job will need and the words he picks from when something breaks.
On the screens that word is the machine's type.

sections.title: Dress it from the type, in one press:

screen.chrome: the editor's maintenance room · the type package
screen.caption: One press, and the machine's type hands down its parts, its plans and the words for a breakdown.

items.lead: Register a machine and give it its type
items.text: One word carries its parts, its service plans, the steps a fitter works through, the spares each job needs and the words he picks from when something breaks.

items.lead: Dress it from the type
items.text: Sets a machine up in one press: its parts, its plans, their checklists, the spares each job needs and the failure words all arrive.

items.lead: Parts arrive ranked by criticality
items.text: The parts a type hands down arrive ranked by how critical each one is.

items.lead: Restore this type's factory parts
items.text: A deleted plan comes back whole with its steps and its tolerances; a type that never had a factory set says so in plain words instead of an error.

items.lead: Change a machine's type
items.text: Refused while a job is open; once that job is finished or cancelled it sheds the old package and takes the new one.

items.lead: The delete dialog names the losses
items.text: It names everything that would die with a machine before you press it.

items.lead: Not a maintained asset
items.text: A vessel or a meter point leaves the maintenance wall and every machine count, and stops reading as somebody's missed maintenance.

items.lead: Change the interval on the machine
items.text: The library is a starting point, never a rule: dressing again is additive, and no interval you changed is ever put back.

items.lead: The type's own failure words
items.text: At the close the cause list is that machine's own, so the ranking of what breaks is never diluted by words somebody typed.

cols: The type copies, it never lends: change the library afterwards and nothing already dressed moves.

sections.title: Meters and plans
sections.promise: A meter nobody types cannot drift.

cols: Running hours and start counts are not typed here.
They are folded from the line's own record of when it ran and when it stopped, so a plan fires on what the machine actually did — not on what somebody remembered to write down.

sections.title: Say when a machine gets serviced:

screen.chrome: the plan pane · when it will fire
screen.caption: The plan says when it will fire, and the same arithmetic that raises the job draws the preview.

items.lead: Meters that keep themselves
items.text: Running hours and starts keep themselves, every shift, with nobody asked and nothing to remember.

items.lead: Correct the offset once
items.text: Every total since corrects itself, and the last-service mark moves by the same amount, so no plan fires early.

items.lead: A machine with no signal of its own
items.text: It works the same plan grammar from a number a person read off it.

items.lead: Five ways a service comes due
items.text: On a date; a set number of days after the last one; every so many running hours or starts; when a signal on the line says it is owed; once a machine has broken down too often.

items.lead: The follow-up born from a signed repair
items.text: Born only when something was actually found; never scanned for and never guessed.

items.lead: The preview cannot disagree with the engine
items.text: The next due date is previewed by the same arithmetic that raises the job.

items.lead: A meter plan's due date reads estimated
items.text: It is projected from the rate the machine is actually running at.

items.lead: A plan with an open job stays quiet
items.text: No second job while the crew is still on the last one, and every job it raises is born a draft for a person to release.

items.lead: The machines wall
items.text: One card per machine: its open jobs, its meters, mean time between failures, mean time to repair, and the downtime behind it.

screens.caption: The ways a service comes due, as the plan pane offers them.
The machines — every machine's open jobs, its running hours against the next service, mean time between failures and mean time to repair.

sections.title: From fault to job
sections.promise: The stop becomes the job in one tap.

cols: A fault that stays in a conversation is a fault nobody can count.
Here the stop, the alarm and the operator's own words all become the same numbered job — and a supervisor decides what happens to it.

sections.title: Turn a stop or an alarm into tracked work:

screen.caption: The door a fault becomes a numbered job through.

items.lead: The board opens on the debt
items.text: Overdue, due today, this week, later, and what the line has asked for.

items.lead: The week the crew walks into
items.text: Seven days from today, protected windows drawn as rooms, anything late pinned to today.

items.lead: Raise it
items.text: Tell maintenance something is wrong: the machine, what is wrong, how bad, whether the line is down because of it.

items.lead: Call maintenance from a stop
items.text: Turns a stop into tracked work: the machine, the moment and the reason ride along, nothing retyped.

items.lead: Call maintenance from an alarm
items.text: The same request carrying the alarm itself, so the job and the alarm can never point at different events.

items.lead: Make it a job
items.text: Turns a real ask into a numbered work order; a request with no machine named is refused until one is.

items.lead: Release does three things at once
items.text: The checklist freezes from the plan, the job goes to a name, and a protected window is booked when the job genuinely stops the line and the plant has left that switch on.

items.lead: Cancel the job, with a reason
items.text: The reason is demanded, and the record keeps it next to who cancelled it and when.

cols: An ask is not a job: nothing is scheduled, nothing is counted and nobody is assigned until a supervisor turns it into one.

screens.caption: The alarm a fitter is called from.
One job opened — why now, the checklist that will freeze, the part the shelf is short of, one press to release.

sections.title: The technician's phone
sections.promise: The phone is the technician's whole tool.

cols: The same application, sized for a hand: nothing to install, nothing licensed per screen, and nothing filed later.
Every press writes at once.

sections.title: Take it, start it, work it, finish it:

screen.chrome: the job screen · on a phone
screen.caption: The frozen checklist with its readings, in a fitter's hand.

items.lead: Filter to mine
items.text: His jobs, late first, each with its machine, why it is due and what the plan expects to find on the shelf.

items.lead: I'll take it
items.text: The job is his; a take can only ever point at the person pressing it, and the name is the state, so there is no badge to look for.

items.lead: A reading judged at the box
items.text: A measurement with a limit is judged in red before anything is sent.

items.lead: A failed step blocks the close
items.text: The job cannot be closed while a required step is failed or unfinished.

items.lead: Take a spare from the step
items.text: Stock moves there and then against this job: no confirmation, no quantity box, no partial take, exactly what the plan froze.

items.lead: The store's own words when the shelf is short
items.text: The store answers the take in its own words instead of failing quietly.

items.lead: A photograph on the step
items.text: Filed with the job and readable for ever; a wrong photograph is answered with a better one, never removed.

items.lead: Finish, then close and sign
items.text: The close books the minutes, prices the labour from the line's own rate, books the parts, moves the counters, records what broke and why, and seals the record.

cols: The checklist freezes at release, so a plan edited next month never rewrites work already in flight.

screens.caption: The jobs board on a phone — the filters, the job rows.
Finishing and closing a job where the machine is.

sections.title: Parts and the shelf
sections.promise: The shelf answers before the technician walks to it.

cols: The store is not a number somebody keeps up to date.
Stock is the sum of every receipt, issue, return and correction — so the shelf can answer a job before the crew is sent to do it.

sections.title: Catalogue a spare or move stock:

screen.chrome: the store · what a job will be short of
screen.caption: The store, read by what a job will be short of.

items.lead: Parts held against the shelf
items.text: A job's expected parts answer ready or short before anyone walks anywhere, with the quantity the plan asked for.

items.lead: Shortages pinned on top
items.text: Each names the jobs it is holding, with its bin and its family.

items.lead: Record a movement
items.text: Received, or corrected with a note: the shelf moves and the running balance shows it.

items.lead: The ledger refuses edits and deletes
items.text: A mistake is corrected by a movement that says so.

items.lead: Bind the need to the spare
items.text: “A mechanical seal” becomes this site's part number and quantity, and the picker puts what this machine actually eats at the top of the list.

items.lead: A spare that belongs to one line
items.text: It leaves every other line's store, its stock report and its shortage count.

items.lead: Stock movements, the whole site's ledger
items.text: Newest first, by day, with the job, the delivery note and the person — and a spreadsheet in one press.

cols: One shelf per site, shared by every line on it, unless a spare is marked as belonging to one line only.

screens.caption: Every hand that touched the shelf — what moved, against which job, and who.
The job's dossier — why now, the checklist that will freeze, the part the shelf is short of.

sections.title: The record
sections.promise: A record nobody signed is a note.

cols: Every close writes a record the plant can hand over: designed once, computed on the server, frozen, numbered, sealed, signed, and printed on the plant's own letterhead.

screen.chrome: the maintenance review · as it prints
screen.caption: The monthly review as SOP prints it, on the plant's own letterhead.

items.lead: 01 Design
items.text: Blocks bound to real rows: the checklist and its readings, the parts a job consumed, done against due, what broke, and each machine's reliability.

items.lead: 02 Compute
items.text: On the server, in the plant's own clock: as each maintenance job closes, every week, every month, or over the range an auditor names.

items.lead: 03 Seal
items.text: Frozen on arrival, numbered, fingerprinted; run it again and you have a second document beside the first, never a refresh.

items.lead: 04 Sign
items.text: By name and capacity, proved with the signer's own password, bound to the fingerprint, never edited and never withdrawn.

items.lead: 05 Deliver
items.text: Printed on the plant's letterhead in three languages, e-mailed to the list, filed as a PDF, exported as a spreadsheet.

items.lead: 0 report servers
items.text: The engine runs on the backend already installed; a small worker files the PDF and posts it.

items.lead: 0 third-party licences
items.text: No reporting product, no rendering licence, no designer bought separately.

sections.title: The sheets a maintenance manager is judged on
cols: The maintenance record — One job on one sheet: its checklist, its readings against their limits, the parts it used and the signature.
The week ahead — What falls due, what is already late, and what part is missing.
The maintenance review — Done against due, what broke, mean time between failures and mean time to repair, what it cost and who did the work.
Bad actors — The worst machines and the worst causes, ranked by the downtime behind them.
The audit sheet — The same numbers narrowed to the machines a person ticked; critical equipment is a list a person ticks, not a flag the software keeps.
Nothing on the sheet is typed — Labour from the minutes the job booked and the line's own rate, parts from the ledger as they were priced the day they were issued.
A dash, and how many — Where a figure was never given the sheet prints a dash and says how many, never a confident zero.
A signed record stays as signed — Or it becomes an openly unsigned one.

screens.caption: The one-job record — numbered, sealed, with the machine, the part and where the job came from.
The month as maintenance is judged on it — what actually breaks, and reliability per machine.

sections.alt: What maintenance gives the rest of the plant, and what it takes from it — solid gives, dashed takes.

sections.title: And what no other platform does like us

items.lead: It opens on a plant that is already there
items.text: Maintenance is not a system you feed; it is arithmetic over the plant the SCADA is already writing, on the same rows.

items.lead: One word plants the whole maintenance package
items.text: The machine's type carries its parts, its plans, their checklists, the spares each job needs and the failure words — and the type copies, it never lends.

items.lead: A meter nobody types cannot drift
items.text: Running hours and starts keep themselves from the line's own record; correct an offset once and every total since corrects itself.

items.lead: The stop becomes the job in one tap
items.text: From the restart receipt or from the alarm acknowledgement, so the job and the alarm can never point at different events.

items.lead: The phone is the technician's whole tool
items.text: Nothing to install, nothing licensed per screen, nothing filed later: every press writes at once.

items.lead: The shelf answers before the technician walks to it
items.text: Stock is the sum of its movements, shortages pinned on top naming the jobs they hold, and the ledger refuses edits and deletes.

items.lead: A record nobody signed is a note
items.text: Computed on the server, frozen, numbered, sealed, signed by name and capacity, never edited and never withdrawn — with no report server and no second database.

items.lead: Nothing to connect, because there is nothing to connect
items.text: A released job books a protected window the performance engine already honours, on the same plan the production orders are laid out on; no meter to transport, no asset register to type, and no nightly job that copies yesterday's plant into a second database.

cols: None of this is an interface between products. It is the same rows, read four ways, under one security model that reaches the printed sheet.
